title: America’s Open-Model Paradox
gist: Chinese open-weight models (Qwen, Kimi, GLM, DeepSeek) have become the default base layer for Western AI builders — Qwen alone went from 1% to 69% of new open-model fine-tunes between January 2024 and February 2026 — because Western labs may lawfully distill from Chinese open weights but are contractually barred from distilling GPT or Claude. Sequoia argues the fix is a legal, metered, audited American 'controlled teacher access' market that sells structured training rights from US frontier labs to verified Western and allied companies, or the West leads the closed frontier while renting the open layer from Beijing.

themes.theme: Chinese open weights as default substrate

insights.claim: Qwen's share of new open-model fine-tunes and adaptations rose from 1% in January 2024 to 69% by February 2026, according to ATOM's Report.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: The open-model derivative stack has effectively standardized on Chinese weights in two years; any US 'open model' policy or product bet must be underwritten against that installed base, not against a level playing field.
insights.quote: Qwen’s share of new open-model fine-tunes and adaptations rose from 1% in January 2024 to 69% by February 2026 according to ATOM’s Report

insights.claim: The majority of American AI startups appear to be using Chinese open weights somewhere in their stack, and the dependence now extends upstream from applications to Western labs themselves.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Diligence question for any AI portfolio company: where in the stack are Chinese weights, and what breaks commercially or in procurement if that becomes restricted or disallowed for defense/regulated buyers.
insights.quote: The majority of American AI startups seem to be using Chinese open weights somewhere in their stack.
insights.locator: The majority of American AI startups

insights.claim: Thinking Machines pre-trained its Inkling model independently but used synthetic data generated by Moonshot's Kimi K2.5 to bootstrap supervised fine-tuning — a Western frontier lab lawfully learning from a Chinese open model.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Concrete proof that Chinese-model dependence has reached the frontier-lab tier, not just the application tier — the strongest single datapoint for the essay's policy ask.
insights.quote: Thinking Machines pre-trained Inkling independently, but used synthetic data generated by Moonshot’s Kimi K2.5 to bootstrap its supervised fine-tuning.

insights.claim: The competitive prize in open models is not model revenue but becoming the substrate on which global enterprises build products, synthetic data, post-training systems, evals, agents and applied AI.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Reframes 'open models don't make money' as a category error — value accrues to whoever owns the default base layer, so measure share of derivative fine-tunes, not licensing revenue.
insights.quote: The prize is to become the substrate on which global enterprises build and improve digital intelligence.
insights.locator: The stakes extend far beyond model revenue

insights.claim: Capability today flows from Western frontier models through alleged unauthorized foreign extraction into Chinese open weights and only then into lawful Western post-training, while the direct route from American frontier models to lawful Western post-training is missing.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: The core mental model of the piece: American IP protection on frontier outputs is currently a subsidy to Chinese open models, because it blocks Americans and not the covert extractor.
insights.quote: Western frontier models → alleged unauthorized foreign extraction → Chinese open weights → lawful Western post-training
insights.locator: The flow today looks something like this

insights.claim: A Western lab has a legal path to learn from a Chinese open model while equivalent use of GPT or Claude outputs is prohibited, making the legal asymmetry — not raw capability — the binding constraint.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Implies terms-of-service enforcement by US labs is strategically self-defeating at the national level; watch for labs or Washington relaxing distillation restrictions for vetted domestic buyers.
insights.quote: a Western lab had a legal path to learn from a Chinese open model, while equivalent use of GPT or Claude outputs is prohibited
insights.locator: The point is that a Western lab

insights.claim: Pre-training creates a capable base model while post-training turns it into a useful coding, reasoning, tool-using and agentic system, and a stronger teacher converts part of that expensive discovery process into a cheaper learning problem.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Explains why teacher access is worth paying for: it converts capex-heavy R&D discovery into cheap supervised learning, which is where marginal cost curves for open models actually bend.
insights.quote: A stronger teacher converts part of that expensive discovery process into a cheaper learning problem.
insights.locator: Pre-training creates a capable base model

insights.claim: Distillation does not explain China's overall open-model lead — Chinese labs have world-class researchers, substantial compute, strong pre-trained models and software-hardware codesign — but it does account for a meaningful share of their advantage specifically over American open models.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: A careful hedge: banning distillation alone will not close the gap, so trades premised on export controls or enforcement 'fixing' Chinese open models are likely to disappoint.
insights.quote: Even if distillation represents a smaller share of  a Chinese model’s total capability, it represents a meaningful share of its advantage over American open models.
insights.locator: Distillation does not explain China’s entire

insights.claim: New enforcement mechanisms will make large-scale distillation harder, slower and more expensive for Chinese companies but will not eliminate distillation backed by state actors, so every Western frontier advance keeps creating another teacher for Chinese labs.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Treat each US frontier release as a forward-dated capability transfer to Chinese open models — the lag between a US frontier launch and a comparable Chinese open release is the metric to track.
insights.quote: Every Western frontier advance therefore creates another teacher for Chinese labs.

insights.claim: Downloading a Chinese model gives a Western company permanent control over that particular version, but because AI capability is an upgrade cycle, if China stops releasing its strongest models existing Western products will not break — they will fall behind.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Reprices the perceived safety of open weights: the risk is not a service cutoff but silent competitive decay, which is far harder to hedge and shows up in product roadmaps a cycle later.
insights.quote: If China stops releasing its strongest models, existing products will not break. They will fall behind.
insights.locator: But AI capability is an upgrade cycle

insights.claim: Reuters reported that Chinese authorities have discussed restricting overseas access to advanced models, including models not yet released, with no final policy announced.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: A live tail risk with an identifiable catalyst: formal Chinese restrictions on open-weight releases would strand Western builders mid-upgrade-cycle and instantly reprice Western open-model efforts.
insights.quote: Chinese authorities have discussed restricting overseas access to advanced models, including models that have not yet been released
insights.locator: Reuters recently reported that Chinese authorities

insights.claim: An open-weight model is not an auditable model: weights are the compressed result of training and do not reveal the pre-training corpus, which data was filtered or poisoned, what training interventions were made, or whether rare trigger-dependent behavior was embedded.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Kills the assumption that 'open' equals 'verifiable' — creates a real market for provenance, model-audit and trusted-supply-chain tooling in regulated AI deployments.
insights.quote: An open-weight model is not necessarily an auditable model.
insights.locator: There is also a more technical security problem

insights.claim: Possessing model weights cannot prove the absence of a backdoor, and research shows deliberately implanted behavior can survive supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and adversarial training — an acceptable supply-chain risk for many consumer apps but not for defense, intelligence or critical infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Draws the commercial line where a domestic open-model vendor can win: government, defense and critical-infrastructure buyers cannot use Chinese weights at any price, creating a protected addressable market.
insights.quote: The point is that possessing the weights cannot prove the absence of one.
insights.locator: We are not alleging that Qwen

themes.theme: Proposed American path: priced teacher access

insights.claim: Without a domestic legal route to convert American frontier capability into cheaper ownable models, the West may lead at the closed frontier while falling into dependence on China for the open layer.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: The central bear case: closed-frontier leadership and open-layer dependence can coexist, so US frontier-lab dominance is not evidence the open-model battle is being won.
insights.quote: Without a domestic route, the West may lead at the closed frontier while falling into dependence on China for the open layer.
insights.locator: American companies need a legal way

insights.claim: Western base-model efforts including Reflection (building open super-intelligence for enterprises and sovereigns), TML and Nemotron are making strong progress, but stronger pre-training alone does not solve the teacher problem.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Names the specific Western open-model contenders to watch, while warning that funding pre-training alone is an incomplete bet without legal access to frontier teachers.
insights.quote: Keep building Western base models: Reflection (building open super-intelligence for enterprises & sovereigns), TML, and Nemotron are making incredible progress.

insights.claim: Frontier labs could sell structured training rights to qualifying Western and allied companies, with access trailing the frontier, covering defined capabilities, limited to verified companies, and metered and audited, while the most sensitive biological and cyber capabilities remain restricted.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: A new revenue line for closed frontier labs — licensed distillation rights — and a potential unlock for the entire Western open-model ecosystem; watch for the first lab to offer it commercially.
insights.quote: It would create a legal, priced route for capability transfer that sophisticated foreign actors are already pursuing covertly.

insights.claim: If a voluntary market for teacher access does not develop, such access could eventually be made a condition attached to major federal AI contracts.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Signals a coercive policy backstop — federal procurement leverage over frontier labs is the escalation path to watch if licensing does not emerge on its own.
insights.quote: If a voluntary market does not develop, access could eventually become a condition attached to major federal AI contracts, for example.
insights.locator: Keep raising the cost of foreign distillation

insights.claim: The precedent for permissive capability transfer is training on the open web: had that not been allowed, there would be no leading AI at all, since all the leading labs benefited from copious openly available data.
insights.speaker: Sequoia Arc
insights.so_what: Uses the web-scraping precedent to argue against tightening IP around model outputs — a policy analogy that cuts against the litigation-driven consensus on training data rights.
insights.quote: Imagine if we had not allowed for training on the open web. We would have no leading AI at all.
